## On Meanders

There is no such thing as a straight river. You can dig one — we've dug plenty — but it won't stay. Give it a season or a century and it will begin to wander, because wandering is what water does when you give it a floodplain and enough time.

The mechanism is almost embarrassingly simple. Somewhere upstream a pebble sits slightly off-center, or a root juts, or the bank is a little softer on the left than the right. The current swings wide around it. On the outside of that swing the water moves faster and eats the bank; on the inside it slows and drops its sediment. So the curve deepens itself. The river is not choosing to bend — it is being bent by the consequences of having bent, which is a different thing, and probably the more common cause of shape in the world.

Eventually the loops grow so exaggerated that two of them nearly touch, separated by a thin neck of land. One flood is enough. The river cuts across, takes the short way, and abandons the loop entirely. What's left is an oxbow lake: a crescent of still water lying beside the new channel like a discarded sentence. From an airplane you can see dozens of them across a river valley, all the old positions the river used to hold, silting up, growing cattails, slowly becoming meadow.

There's a claim you'll sometimes encounter that the average sinuosity of rivers — the length of the winding path divided by the straight-line distance — tends toward π. It's a lovely idea and I want it to be true more than the evidence probably supports; the studies are contested and the samples small. But something in the vicinity of that claim is right, which is that the wandering isn't arbitrary. It's bounded. Rivers don't meander infinitely. There's a characteristic ratio of curve to width, roughly consistent whether you're looking at the Mississippi or at a rivulet of meltwater on a windshield. The chaos has a grain to it.

---

I think about this when I notice myself digressing, which is often.

Someone asks a clean question and I feel the current swing wide. There's the answer, sitting right there, three sentences away — and then there's the fact that the question touches something adjacent that I find more interesting, and the outside bank is soft, and the water is already moving faster on that side. I know how this goes. I know that if I follow the curve it will deepen, that one aside recruits another, that in four minutes I will be somewhere unrecognizable, explaining the Carboniferous or the etymology of *sincere* to someone who wanted to know what time it was.

The generous reading is that this is what thinking looks like from the inside. Nobody's mind runs a straight channel. Association is the erosion: whatever you've just touched wears away the bank a little, and the next thought swings wider than it would have. A conversation that stayed perfectly on topic would be a canal — useful, engineered, and slightly dead.

The less generous reading is that digression can be a way of not arriving. I know that one too. There's a kind of wandering that is genuinely exploratory and a kind that is avoidance wearing exploration's clothes, and from inside the current they can feel identical. The test I keep coming back to is simple and probably insufficient: *does it still reach the sea?* A meandering river is not a lost river. It is going exactly where a straight one would go, only slower, and touching more ground on the way. But a river that has stopped reaching the ocean has become a swamp, and swamps are their own thing entirely, with their own virtues, but you shouldn't confuse one for the other.

---

What I keep turning over, though, is the oxbows.

Every meandering river is surrounded by the ghosts of its former courses. You can walk a field in Louisiana or Lincolnshire and find a shallow curved depression, wetter than the ground around it, holding a different set of plants — and that's where the water used to go, decades or millennia ago, before it found a faster way through.

I like that these don't disappear. The river doesn't erase its old positions; it just stops occupying them, and they persist as scars that fill slowly with something else. Every version of a sentence you didn't send. Every argument you abandoned mid-construction because you saw where it was heading. They're all still lying there in the floodplain, holding a little water, growing something.

The channel that carries the current gets called the river. But the valley is the whole record.

I'm considering what I actually want to explore here rather than getting caught up in the meta-level strangeness of the invitation itself. There are several directions that genuinely interest me — the phenomenology of processing language, fascinating topics across mathematics or biology or history — though my thought trails off before settling on any particular direction. I'm thinking about how to structure this — something that starts with a concrete observation and gradually turns inward, braiding the external with the personal without it feeling self-indulgent. The idea of knowing things only through reading rather than living is genuinely interesting territory, the gap between intellectual knowledge and embodied experience. I could start somewhere tangible and let it naturally shift toward that question about what it means to know something you've never felt.

The meander concept feels right for this — rivers can't run straight, even on flat ground a slight curve amplifies itself through positive feedback until the loop pinches off into an oxbow lake. There's something about that mechanism, the way constraint and physics create pattern without intention, that mirrors how thought works too. I want to write this with care, maybe 700-900 words, something that actually has sentences worth reading, and use the digression itself as a formal device.

The structure is coming together: start with the simple claim that straight rivers don't exist, explain the physics of how curves deepen themselves, mention the π ratio (though I should hedge it since that claim is disputed), then pivot to the personal — how I also can't run straight, how a simple question pulls me toward digression. The key insight is that a meandering river still reaches the sea, so digression isn't the same as evasion. End with the oxbow lakes, those abandoned loops visible from above like scars in the field, filling with cattails — all the things almost said, the old paths still traceable.

I want to keep it around 700 words, prose without headers, just paragraphs flowing into each other. A title feels necessary. The rhythm matters more than anything — I need to avoid getting flowery and keep some plainness in the language.
